WIND, OCEAN CURRENT AND CYCLONE

  • They are found between 10°N and 10°S.
  • The Doldrums overlap with the ITCZ region.

Horse Latitude

  • Horse latitudes are regions located about 30°N and 30°S of the equator.
  • It is an area of subtropical high.
  • It is a high-pressure area at divergence of trade winds and westerlies.
  • They are characterised by Sunny skies, calm winds, and a very little precipitation.

LOCAL WINDS

  • Local winds are winds that occur in a specific area and are caused by local temperature differences, topography, or other geographical features.

Types of Local Winds

WindsWarm/Cold WindPlace where it Blows
ChinookIt is warm, dry wind and is also known as "Snow Eaters" because it melt snow coverCanada, eastern side of Rockies
SiroccoIt is warm, hot, and dry wind. It also causes "blood rain"Sahara (North Africa) → Mediterranean / Southern Europe (corrected: Siberia/Canada/US → Sahara, Mediterranean)
KhamsinIt is hot, dry, and dusty windEgypt / Levant / North Africa (corrected: Gulf of Guinea → Egypt)
HarmattanThey are dry, dusty warm winds. These winds are also known as "Dr. Wind"West Africa (Sahara → Gulf of Guinea) (corrected: Egypt/Sahara → West Africa)
BrickfielderIt is hot, dry, and dusty windAustralia
BlizzardThey are very cold and carry snowNorth America (USA, Canada) / polar regions (corrected: Australian Desert → North America)
MistralThese are strong, cold, and dry windsFrance
BoraThese are strong and cold windsAdriatic Sea
Foehn/FohnIt is warm and dry wind (downslope wind on the lee side of a mountain)Alps (especially northern side of the Alps, also Rocky Mountains) (corrected: cold → warm; Föhn is warm)
PamperoThese are cold windsPampas region, Argentina

Map 1: Warm and Cold Winds

Land Breeze and Sea Breeze

  • Land Breeze and Sea Breeze are types of local winds that occur due to temperature difference between land and water.

Land Breeze

  • It occurs at night when land cools faster than sea, creating high-pressure over land and low pressure over the sea, causing air to move from land to sea; more common in autumn and winter.

Sea Breeze

  • It occurs during the day when land heats up faster than the sea, creating low pressure over land and high-pressure over the sea, causing air to move from sea to land; more common in spring and summer.

CYCLONE

  • Cyclones are rotating mass of air.
  • They are large, powerful storm that forms over warm ocean waters, with strong winds and heavy rain.

Formation of Cyclones

  • Cyclones form when warm, moist air rises over the ocean. As the air rises, it creates low pressure, and cooler air rushes in to replace it. The Earth's rotation causes the air to spin, and the storm grows stronger. When the storm gets big enough, it becomes a cyclone with strong winds and heavy rain.
  • A cyclone rotates anti-clockwise in Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in Southern Hemisphere.

Favorable Conditions for Formation of Cyclone

  • Large sea surface temperature
  • Atmospheric Instability
  • Coriolis Force
  • Pre-existing weak low pressure area

Different Names of Cyclones around the World

  • Hurricane: Atlantic Ocean
  • Typhoon: South China Sea and Western Pacific Ocean
  • Willy-Willy: Australia
  • Cyclone: India
During cyclone, Cumulonimbus clouds are formed with extensive vertical development.

WIND, OCEAN CURRENT AND CYCLONE

Tropical and Temperate Cyclone (Extra-Tropical Cyclone)

Tropical CycloneTemperate Cyclone
They originate over seaThey originate over sea and land
They are formed due to certain favourable condition over the sea, as mentioned aboveThey are formed due to frontogenesis i.e. where the warm and cold air mass meet each other
They cover less area but cause major destructionThey cover large area but cause less destruction
They occur rarelyThey occur frequently
They move from east to westThey move from west to east

Anticyclone

  • An anticyclone is formed around an area of high pressure where the air sinks, causing clear skies and calm weather. It usually brings dry, sunny conditions.
  • An anticyclone rotates clockwise in Northern Hemisphere and anti-clockwise in Southern Hemisphere.

OCEAN CURRENTS

  • Ocean currents are large movements of water in the ocean that flow in a specific direction.
  • Ocean water moves in two directions: horizontally and vertically.
  • Horizontal movements are referred to as currents, while vertical changes are called upwellings or downwellings.

Reasons for Movement of Ocean Currents

  1. 1. Wind
  2. 2. Density difference
  3. 3. Gravity
  4. 4. Coriolis force
  5. 5. Coast line
  • Cold water moves from Poles to Equator.
  • Warm water moves from Equator to Poles.

Warm Ocean Currents

  • Brazil, Mozambique, Agulhas, Gulf Stream, Alaska, Norwegian, Kuroshio, E. Australia.

Effects of Ocean Currents

  1. 1. Cold ocean currents: They largely contribute to the formation of coastal deserts in west coast regions of tropical and sub-tropical continents. This is because the cold water makes the air above it cooler and less able to hold moisture.
  2. 2. Warm ocean currents + Cold ocean currents: Together they create best fishing zones due to deposition of planktons. The meeting of warm and cold ocean currents also creates fog that is dangerous for harbouring.
